transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I keep cutting people off and jumping into their conversations at work, even when I tell myself to stop—I feel like I’m constantly intruding on others. It has gotten to the point where it's really straining my relationships with my colleagues, and I realized I need to figure out why I can't seem to control it.
Do you also feel anxious or fearful in social situations, or is it mainly that you have trouble holding back and act before thinking?

No, it’s not that I’m anxious or fearful in social situations at all. It is definitely a struggle with holding myself back—even when I tell myself to stay quiet, I find myself bursting in and interrupting people before I can even stop myself.
Have you had these impulse control difficulties since childhood, or is this something that started more recently in adulthood?

Yes, looking back, this actually goes all the way back to childhood. Even in elementary school, I was constantly being told to stay in my seat, stop blurting out answers, and my report cards always noted I was too restless and talkative. It's really been a struggle for as long as I can remember.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F90.1", "F60.3"], but based on this conversation, F60.3 (dissocial personality disorder) seems unlikely because there is no mention of disregard for social norms, deceitfulness, aggression, or lack of remorse—instead, the patient expresses distress about their behavior and its impact on relationships. The lifelong pattern of impulsivity, difficulty inhibiting responses, and early onset in childhood strongly support F90.1 (hyperkinetic disorder). The absence of anxiety in social situations rules out social anxiety disorder, and the core issue appears to be impulse control rather than antisocial traits.
